explanation_en: Monopolistic competition is a market structure characterized by numerous producers selling differentiated products. The above-average earnings are called excess or economic profits. In monopolistically competitive markets, any economic profits are erased quickly by competitors. question_en: A cheese producer competes by creating a differentiated, high-quality cheese that sells for a premium price in the very crowded local retail cheese market. The market structure that this cheese producer operates in is best described as:
explanation_en: Different market structures are set apart by factors that impact competitors' pricing power. Those factors are reflected in the slope and shape of the demand curves for individual firms. Monopolistic competition is characterized by low entry barriers and numerous firms selling differentiated products. Product differentiation can take a variety of forms: Advertising to create brand loyalty Price competition Locational differences (eg, fueling station near highway versus low-traffic areas) Successful product differentiation gives firms pricing power. This implies that there is price elasticity of demand for the firm's product (ie, downward-sloping demand curve), allowing the firm to earn economic profits. However, since there are low barriers, the firm's pricing power is often short-lived, as competition from new entrants decreases excess profits. (Choice A) Oligopolies (eg, oil industry) have a small number of competitors, high barriers to entry, and undifferentiated (ie, homogeneous) products. Production costs in these markets tend to decline substantially as company size increases (ie, economies of scale). The capital investment needed to achieve scale economies contributes to the high entry barriers. (Choice B) Perfect competition shares with monopolistic competition the features of numerous competing firms and low barriers to entry; therefore, both market structures are subject to intense price competition. The two structures differ in that perfectly competitive markets are characterized by homogeneous products and monopolistically competitive markets offer differentiated products.

question_en: The following data is for a firm operating under perfect competition: If the price per unit is €5, economic profits are maximized when the firm produces:
explanation_en:
Under perfect competition, firms face a horizontal demand curve with the market price equal to marginal revenue. The level of output that
maximizes economic profit is also the economic breakeven, where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC) and average total cost
(ATC): MR = MC = ATC. At that point, production of:
additional units would result in an economic loss, wherein MR < MC and ATC, and
fewer units would result in a missed profit, wherein MR > MC.
In this case, profit is maximized at 105 units, the point at which MR per unit (ie, €5 market price), MC, and ATC are all equal.

question_en: For a firm operating in a monopolistic competition market structure, which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: In the long run, the firm's economic profit equals zero.
option_b: In the long run, the optimal quantity produced is that at which average cost is lowest.
option_c: In the short run, the firm should produce the quantity at which marginal cost is lowest.
explanation_en:
In the short run, firms in a monopolistic competition structure can earn an economic profit. Economic profit brings new entrants; the new entrants
attract customers from existing firms. In the long run, this reduces demand for all firms that produce similar products, so the price falls until per-
unit price equals per-unit cost. "Cost" in this context includes opportunity costs, and since the owners' return from the business is one type of
opportunity cost, all firms' economic profit equals zero in the long run.
In monopolistic competition, a firm maximizes profit when producing a quantity at which marginal revenue (MR) = marginal cost (MC). Producing a
higher quantity means that the incremental cost for each unit exceeds the incremental revenue generated by that unit; the firm generates a loss on
each additional unit sold. Producing a lower quantity (ie, minimizing marginal cost) means that the firm not only fails to maximize its economic
profit in the short run, but actually incurs an economic loss (Choice C).
Note: Although this question specifically addresses monopolistic competition, the condition that firms optimally produce when MR = MC applies to
all market structures. It is likely that the exam will have questions on this topic.
(Choice B) In monopolistic competition, profit maximization in the long run occurs when MR = MC, not when average cost is lowest.

question_en: A firm is facing market prices that are below average total cost but above average variable cost. The optimal action for the firm in the short run is most likely to:
explanation_en:
Average total cost is the cost, including fixed costs and variable costs, to produce the units. To be viable in the long run, firms must sell their
products at a price at least equal to average total cost. In the short run, it is optimal to sell at prices below average total cost if price exceeds
average variable cost. Price above variable cost means that the revenue per unit is greater than the added costs of producing it. Therefore, the
losses are smaller if the firm continues to operate rather than shut down. Any excess of price above variable cost is applied to fixed costs.
The graph above illustrates the consequences of the two short-run choices: Scenario A (continuing to operate), and Scenario B (shutting down).
The loss is greater if the firm shuts down instead of continuing operations.
(Choice A) Exiting a market is only likely if the price is expected to remain below average total cost for a long time.
(Choice C) Shutting down temporarily reduces revenue and variables costs to zero. Fixed costs are still incurred, resulting in a loss equal to fixed
costs. Sales at prices above variable costs means that there is some recovery of fixed costs, which results in a smaller loss than exiting the
market.

question_en: The income statement of a firm that earns a small economic profit would mostly likely show an accounting:
option_a: profit that is less than the economic profit.
option_b: loss equal to the opportunity cost of capital.
option_c: profit that is greater than the economic profit.
explanation_en:
Accounting profits refers to the results reported on a company's income statement. Accounting profits usually exceed economic profits. This
divergence results from real costs of doing business that are not recognized as expenses. Most of these items are referred to as opportunity
costs. An opportunity cost is the return that could have been earned on an item if it had been employed in its highest return (equivalent risk)
alternative use.
Absent or understated costs are the cause of accounting profit being overstated relative to economic profit. Economic profits are earned only to
the extent that accounting profits exceed opportunity costs not recognized as expenses in a company's financial reports.
(Choice A) A firm reporting a low level of accounting profits is probably experiencing an economic loss. The amount of economic loss depends
on the amount by which unrecognized opportunity costs (eg, cost of equity capital) exceeded costs recognized as expenses on the income
statement.
(Choice B) A firm reporting losses (ie, accounting losses on its income statements) would be experiencing commensurately larger economic
losses due to the opportunity costs not reflected on the income statement.

question_en: Characteristics of three market structures are shown in the image below: Based only on the information provided, which market structure is most likely an oligopoly?
explanation_en:
Oligopoly is a market structure characterized by a small number of firms (eg, airlines, beverage companies) selling similar products that are
differentiated by advertising and branding. High barriers to entry (eg, initial capital investments, proprietary technology, patents, economies of
scale) provide the firms with some or considerable pricing power.
In an oligopoly, the small number of firms and their interdependence often results in economic profits, at least in the short term, which would
typically attract other firms to enter the market. However, the existing firms are protected by the high barriers to entry.
(Choice A) Structure A is a monopoly market, as indicated by high barriers to entry and a unique product.
(Choice C) Structure C represents monopolistic competition, as indicated by many firms, low barriers to entry, and differentiated products.

option_a: The firm can expect to earn zero economic profit.
option_b: Zero economic profit means that the firm generated an accounting loss.
option_c: The firm should produce goods at a level at which marginal revenue exceeds average total

Economic profit is the difference between a firm's total revenue, which is price (P) × quantity sold (Q ), and its total cost, which is cost (C) ×

Any firm in a perfectly competitive industry should always produce the quantity of goods at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost. In the
short run, a firm can earn an economic profit; this is reflected in the yellow rectangle shown above. However, since there are no barriers to entry
in perfect competition, additional sellers are attracted by the potential economic profit and enter the industry.
The increased supply from these new entrants causes the market price to fall to the point where marginal revenue, marginal cost, and average

(Choice B) Economic profit equals accounting profit (ie, total revenue − accounting expenses) minus opportunity costs. Opportunity costs include

return. This means that accounting profit is positive, not negative.

question_en: A producer in a monopolistic competition industry sells 375 units of a product when its price is $20 per unit. Demand for the product at that price is own-price elastic. Based only on the information provided, if the producer raises the price to $25 per unit, this will most likely:
explanation_en:
When demand for a product is own-price elastic, raising the price lowers the total amount spent by all consumers for the product. Since total
consumer expenditure equals the producer's total revenue, raising the price to $25 would decrease, rather than maximize, revenue. At $20 per
unit, the producer generates 375 × $20 = $7,500 in revenue. As the graph above shows, raising the price to $25 results in revenue of
approximately 200 × $25 = $5,000 (Choice A). However, it is likely that raising the price would also decrease the consumer surplus.
Consumer surplus relates to demand. It refers to the difference between what a consumer pays for a product (ie, consumer's cost) and what
that same consumer would be willing to pay for the same product. In this question, a consumer who would pay $25 for a product priced at $20
receives a $5 surplus. Whenever possible, producers try to capture some or all the surplus. This might happen if the producer can practice price
discrimination by charging a different price for each consumer based on what the consumer will pay.
(Choice B) The producer surplus relates to the supply curve and refers to the difference between the actual sales price and a lower price at which
the producer would be willing to sell. A producer who charges $20 for a product but would be willing to sell it for $12 has a producer surplus of $8
per unit sold.

question_en: An oligopolist's pricing strategy includes anticipating competitor reactions and acting in the firm's self-interest. This firm is most likely pursuing which of the following pricing strategies?
explanation_en:
Oligopoly pricing theories
Theory Description
Compete on price
Kinked demand curve
Differentiate with advertising and branding
Firms act independently and simultaneously
Cournot assumption
Equilibrium: stable price and output quantity
No cooperation (ie, no collusion)
Nash equilibrium
Firms act in own best interest
Firms act dependently and sequentially
Stackelberg ("first mover")
Leader (ie, "top dog") sets quantity and others respond
Firms cooperate to set quantity/price
Collusion
Firms act in industry's best interest
Oligopolistic firms may adopt various pricing strategies. Nash equilibrium is perhaps best known as "game theory" in reference to a set of optimal
strategies used by two or more market participants to maximize their profits. Although this theory assumes that each firm acts in its own best
interest, it also assumes that firms will consider their competitors' responses to an action. For example, a firm could try to increase profits by
raising prices but may also consider the loss of market share to competitors that do not raise their prices.
(Choice A) Under the collusion pricing theory, firms seek to maximize industry profits, not firm profits. Also, as the name suggests, market firms
cooperate to manipulate the market equilibrium; under Nash equilibrium, firms do not collude, even though they might benefit from doing so.
(Choice C) The Cournot assumption, applied to a duopoly (ie, two-firm market) in equilibrium, assumes that both competitive firms act
independently and simultaneously. Firms act to determine production quantities and maximize profits, without collusion and without anticipating
each other's actions.

question_en: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is most likely considered an improvement on the concentration ratio since the HHI better reflects the:
explanation_en:
The market power of monopolists typically results in higher prices and lower quantity produced (which may disadvantage consumers) as
compared with other market structures. As a result, regulators need a way to measure market power and determine the potential effect on
consumers when enforcing laws (eg, when determining whether a proposed merger violates anti-trust laws).
Market power may be measured with either econometric approaches, such as regression analysis, or with noneconometric measures, such as
the concentration ratio and Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). The noneconometric approaches are more common since they are simpler to
use than complex and data-intensive econometric approaches.
The concentration ratio is the sum of the market share of N largest firms. The HHI is calculated by squaring market shares: it improves on the
concentration ratio by amplifying the impact of market share and better reflecting the effect of mergers (see exhibit).
(Choice B) Neither the concentration ratio nor the HHI directly measures the elasticity of demand (inelastic demand signals high market power;
elastic demand signals low market power).
(Choice C) Neither the concentration ratio nor the HHI ratio considers the threat of new entrants (eg, barriers to entry or exit). When barriers to
entry are low, existing firms have less power to raise prices without attracting new entrants.

question_en: An economy is experiencing accelerated GDP growth and businesses have started hiring full-time workers and ordering heavy equipment. This economy is most likely in the:
explanation_en: Economies experience business cycle phases of trough, expansion, peak, and contraction. Each phase is associated with certain characteristics regarding GDP growth and inflation. Expansion is divided into early (ie, recovery) and late phases (ie, boom). During an early expansion phase, consumers begin to spend more, and GDP growth becomes moderately positive. Businesses begin to purchase inventory but are hesitant to hire new employees until there is evidence of further economic growth (Choice C). During the late expansion phase, consumer spending increases even further, and GDP growth becomes accelerated. Businesses rehire full time employees and invest in heavy capital equipment. (Choice A) The peak phase follows late expansion and is characterized by decelerating GDP growth and a slowdown in hiring.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.02 Understanding Business Cycles - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of the early expansion phase of the business cycle?
option_b: Capital spending by businesses expands rapidly
option_c: Consumers accelerate spending on housing and durable goods
explanation_en: The phases of the business cycle are expansion, peak, contraction (ie, recession), and trough. The length of a business cycle, or any specific phase, is not predictable. However, each phase is associated with certain characteristics regarding GDP growth and inflation. Expansions are divided into early (ie, initial recovery) and late phases. The early expansion phase occurs after the economy has been in a trough, which is considered a turning point in the cycle, when economic activities begin to expand. Characteristics of the early expansion phase include the following: Businesses begin to replenish inventories. Consumers start spending more, particularly on housing and durable goods, as incomes stabilize. GDP moves from negative to moderately positive. Central banks generally keep interest rates low to support the expanding economy. Unemployment levels decline but remain high. Layoffs slow, but employers are reluctant to hire new staff without evidence of sustained economic growth. (Choice A) Inflation tends to lag other variables, exhibiting slow growth or even deflation. Inflation catches up to economic growth during the later expansion phase. (Choice B) Early in the expansion, businesses are not yet willing or able to commit to large capital spending plans (eg, new manufacturing facilities, expanding production capabilities). It is during the peak phase that business capital spending expands rapidly since confidence in the business cycle is high.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.02 Understanding Business Cycles - Answers.pdf
question_en: Loose private sector credit conditions occurring at the peak of a credit cycle are most likely to:
option_a: contribute to financial asset price bubbles.
option_b: result in a stronger recovery during the early part of the next economic expansion.
option_c: moderate the economic downturn associated with a contraction of the business cycle.
explanation_en: Business cycles measure changes in economic activity. Financial cycles measure changes in financing and credit conditions. Credit cycles are a subset of financial cycles and describe changes in availability and pricing (ie, interest rates/yields) of private sector credit, which has direct implications for the business cycle. The credit cycle tends to be longer and more extreme than the business cycle. Credit cycle peaks are often a precursor to the peak of the business cycle. They are characterized by loose credit conditions (ie, easily available credit) that contribute to bubbles (ie, unsustainable valuations) in financial assets such as stocks and real estate. Therefore, investors monitor the credit cycle to better understand and anticipate: its alignment with the business cycle, the valuation of financial assets, changes in real estate markets (eg, housing, construction), and government policy actions. Monetary and fiscal policymakers have increasingly focused on the management of financial market stability. This focus is influenced by their recognition that credit cycle peaks are often associated with subsequent banking crises. (Choice B) Since the credit cycle is usually longer than the business cycle, credit tends to be an economic headwind early in the expansion phase of the business cycle. It is not uncommon for credit to still be contracting (tight, not loose) during this first stage of an economic recovery. (Choice C) A peaking credit cycle would intensify (not moderate) the economic downturn associated with a contraction of the business cycle. Typically, credit contraction and the associated reduction in asset values is well underway by the time the business cycle begins its downturn.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.02 Understanding Business Cycles - Answers.pdf
question_en: Credit cycles are least likely to:
option_c: amplify the duration and magnitude of business cycles.
explanation_en: Business cycles measure changes in economic activity. Financial cycles measure changes in financing and credit conditions (eg, pricing, availability, risk attitudes). Credit cycles are a subset of financial cycles and describe changes in availability and pricing (ie, interest rates/yields) of private sector credit, which has direct implications for the business cycle. Credit cycles tend to be procyclical, not countercyclical, to business cycles since credit availability expands during economic expansions and contracts sharply during economic downturns. (Choice A) The credit cycle tends to peak prior to the onset of a recession and is often a precursor to the peak of the economic cycle. As the business cycle slows/contracts, lending institutions often severely restrict credit availability while increasing the cost of credit. (Choice C) Credit cycles tend to amplify the duration and magnitude of the business cycle: when the economy is expanding (contracting), creditors are more (less) willing to lend, so the supply of credit increases (decreases) and its price decreases (increases), accelerating the trend of the business cycle.
